verses.1:
Al-Mizan presents the verse as the first part of a decisive proof of resurrection and recompense. God’s comprehensive ownership and rule over everything in heaven and earth mean that He may dispose of creation as He wills: creating, sustaining, causing death, restoring life, and requiting deeds. The following verse supplies the proof’s second premise, His complete knowledge, so the two verses introduce the ensuing account of resurrection and reward.

Praise for Him in the hereafter corresponds to praise for His visible worldly order in the heavens and earth; the earthly order will be replaced in the hereafter. His being Wise and khabīr shows that His governance of this world and then the hereafter rests on wisdom and awareness. Wisdom requires an afterlife, lest creation be vain and the righteous remain undistinguished from corrupters and the mindful from the depraved. By His awareness, God will gather every being without omission and recompense each soul for what it earned. Khabīr denotes knowledge of a thing’s particulars and is thus more specific than ʿalīm, “knowledgeable.”
verses.2: Al-Mizan explains that yaliju and yakhruju, “goes down into” and “emerges,” are opposites, as are yanzilu, “descends,” and yaʿruju, “ascends.” Together these opposing movements figuratively express God’s knowledge of every movement and act of every motile being. His being merciful and forgiving indicates that His mercy is firmly fixed and that, on account of faith, His forgiveness extends to a people.
verses.3:
Al-Mizan says that the disbelievers deny the Final Hour, al-sāʿah, or resurrection, despite God’s evident all-encompassing reign and knowledge. The Prophet is therefore commanded to swear by his Lord, the Knower of the unseen, that the Hour will surely come.

Their difficulty is that decomposed bodies mingle with other bodies and their matter assumes new forms; having never seen their scattered parts separated and reassembled, they judge resurrection impossible. God’s knowledge, from which not even an atom’s weight escapes, refutes this. Everything, whether smaller or larger, is inscribed in a clear, unchanging, undying book, even when its material form has vanished from the physical world.
verses.4: Al-Mizan explains that the li- in li-yajzī is causal and connects to “it shall come to you” (34:3): the Hour will come in order that God may reward. This gives one of the two reasons for resurrection: those who believe and do good will receive forgiveness and gracious sustenance, namely Paradise and all it contains. This description parallels “He is merciful, forgiving” (34:2); the other reason is indicated in the next verse.
verses.5:
Al-Mizan explains saʿaw, from saʿī, as strenuous walking, and muʿājizīn as an intensive form of iʿjāz, “to render weak or incapable”; it may also mean competing or racing. The expression is metaphorical: the deniers rush at God’s signs as though toward goal-posts, seeking to disable God and outstrip Him.

Rijz means rijs, “filth,” and may refer to their wicked acts, making the revulsive punishment a requital for, or consequence of, those acts; it is also said to mean a terrible punishment. The verse alludes to the disbelievers who persist in denying the resurrection.
verses.6:
Al-Mizan explains that those given knowledge are people who know God and His signs, and that what was revealed to the Prophet is the Qur’an. Grammatically, they see is followed by what has been revealed as its first object and the truth as its second. The statement may begin a new contrast between the knowledgeable and the disbelievers, or be an adverbial clause concerning the disbelievers: they deny the Hour in ignorance, whereas those who know God and His signs recognize the revealed Qur’an, which announces the Hour, as truth.

The Qur’an also guides to the path of the Mighty, the Praised. God is Mighty because He is never vanquished and His will prevails; He is Praised because all His acts remain good and beautiful despite His might. These names contrast with the futile attempt of some people to weaken God or thwart His signs.
verses.7: Al-Mizan says that the disbelievers’ phrase “a man” mockingly refers to the Prophet, whom they know is warning people of resurrection and recompense. Muzziqtum means to be torn apart or ruptured, here rendered “scattered about,” while khalqin jadīd means a new, stable, enduring form: after annihilation at death, they would be revived and created anew. The clause “when you have been scattered about” adverbially qualifies their becoming a new creation. Thus they ridicule his claim that, once their dust-like remains have become so dispersed as to be indistinguishable from other things, they will be recreated and restored to being.
verses.8:
Al-Mizan explains that the disbelievers express astonishment at the claim that decomposed bodies will be reassembled. In their view, the Prophet must either knowingly forge a lie about God in order to mislead people, or be insane and speak without sound judgment.

The verse rejects this supposed pair of alternatives: he is neither lying nor mad. Rather, those who disbelieve in the hereafter are themselves in punishment and great error. Their punishment will become manifest to them, and their deep misguidance has prevented their intellects from grasping and accepting the truth. Their lack of faith in the hereafter is the reason they have fallen into this punishment and error.
verses.9:
Al-Mizan says that the verse warns those who accuse the Prophet of lying about God’s signs and mock him. “What is before them and behind them” conveys that heaven and earth encompass them: wherever they look, the sky is above them and the earth bears them, leaving no escape.

Because the earth and sky obey God’s command, He could, if He willed, swallow them into the earth or send fragments of heaven down upon them and destroy them. This possibility is a sign for every servant who obediently turns to his Lord. Only the arrogant, too puffed up to turn or return to God, mock these matters or charge the Prophet with lying about the divine signs.
verses.10: Al-Mizan explains faḍl as a gift and awwibī as echoing back voices in God’s glorification, not as travelling or physically following David. The command to the mountains and birds indirectly states that David was given control over them so that they would join him in praise. God also made iron pliant for him despite its natural stiffness.
verses.11: Al-Mizan explains sābighāt as coats of mail and sard as their chain-links. David was commanded to make large armor with links properly proportioned. The command to work righteousness explains why iron was made yielding to him: these blessings were meant to be answered with gratitude expressed through righteous deeds, under God’s watchful sight.
verses.12: Al-Mizan explains that the wind was subjected to Solomon, travelling a month’s distance from daybreak to noon and another month’s distance from noon to eventide. God also melted qiṭr, copper, so that it flowed like a fountain. Some, not all, of the jinn were put under Solomon’s control by God’s permission and worked before him; those who deviated from God’s command by disobeying Solomon were made to taste a worldly punishment of fire.
verses.13: Al-Mizan explains that the jinn made for Solomon prayer-niches, statues, immense serving-basins like reservoirs, and huge cauldrons fixed in place. The command to give thanks addresses Solomon and the kin of David with him, requiring them to work and worship God gratefully. That few servants are thankful either elevates the rare grateful servants or urges an increase in their number.
verses.14: Al-Mizan reports that, according to narrations, dābbat al-arḍ means a termite, while minsaʾah means a staff. Solomon died while standing and leaning on his staff, so neither people nor jinn recognized his death for a time. God sent a termite to eat the staff; when it broke and Solomon fell, the jinn learned of his death. This showed that they did not know the unseen, for otherwise they would not have continued in humiliating drudgery after he died.
verses.15: Al-Mizan identifies Sabaʾ as pure-blooded Arabs from Yemen, said to be named after Sabaʾ ibn Yashjub ibn Yaʿrub ibn Qaḥṭān. The two gardens lay to the right and left of their dwellings. Eating their Lord’s sustenance means living from those gardens and thanking God for His blessings. Their land was suitable and wholesome, and their forgiving Lord did not take them to account for their shortcomings.
verses.16: Al-Mizan takes ʿArim to mean a dam, while noting that some interpret it as torrential rain. Because the people of Sabaʾ abandoned the gratitude they had been commanded to show, God flooded their land, destroyed their gardens, and replaced them with growth yielding bitter fruit, tamarisk, and only a small number of lote-trees.
verses.17: Al-Mizan explains that “this” refers to the flood and replacement of Sabaʾ’s gardens. While jazāʾ can denote requital broadly, al-mujāzāh is used only for an evil consequence. The verse therefore may mean that Sabaʾ were requited in this way for abandoning gratitude, or that God requites no one with evil except one extremely ungrateful for His blessings.
verses.18: Al-Mizan explains that “between them” refers to Sabaʾ, and that the blessed towns are those of Syria. The intervening towns were close enough to be visible from one another and were evenly spaced for travel. God thus made travel through them safe by night or day, without fear or apprehension.
verses.19:
Al-Mizan explains that Sabaʾ had abundant produce, nearby waystations, safe roads, easy travel, and prosperity, but grew weary of these blessings and asked that their journeys be lengthened through deserts and wilds. Their request was ungrateful wrongdoing and implicitly sought the destruction of their towns. Since they refused to recognize God’s blessings in travel as in their settlements, God gave them what they sought by destroying their land and scattering their people.

They and their ruins vanished until only names and legends remained; their complete dispersal became proverbial. Their story is a sign for those who are abundantly patient in God’s way and grateful for His many blessings. It shows that people must worship their Lord in gratitude and face a day of resurrection and recompense for their deeds.
verses.20: Al-Mizan connects Iblīs’s opinion being proved true with his claim that he would deceive and misguide people and that most would not be grateful. It may mean either that he succeeded in deceiving them or that he discovered his claim to be true of them. Their following him, except for a group of believers, explains how his opinion proved true. “Them” refers to people generally, not solely to Sabaʾ, though the verse includes them.
verses.21:
Al-Mizan explains that Iblīs had no power to compel people; they freely chose to follow him and thereby gave him authority over themselves. They therefore have no excuse or ground to claim compulsion. Their following him arose from doubt about the hereafter, rooted in their hearts and manifested in obedience to him. God allowed Iblīs authority only to the extent that they ceded it, so that believers in the hereafter might be distinguished from those who doubt it, without removing responsibility for their choice.

“Save that We might distinguish” means distinction between the two groups, not a literal acquisition of knowledge. The expression states the ultimate purpose of their yielding to Iblīs in place of directly saying that he had authority only over those who let him control them. Faith and doubt concerning the hereafter are specified because faith in the hereafter restrains sin and impels obedience, whereas belief in God and His Messenger alone would not do so without it. God’s preservation of all things means that nothing escapes His knowledge, and implicitly warns against ingratitude and wrongdoing.
verses.22:
Al-Mizan explains that the Prophet is commanded to challenge the alleged gods: call on those whom the idolaters have sworn to be gods besides Allah and ask them for what is needed. Their failure to answer shows that they possess no control, even of an atom’s-weight, in the heavens or earth. A being deserves lordship or worship only if it controls something people need and can bestow it upon them; one that controls nothing is neither god nor lord.

The verse also denies the idolaters’ claim that God’s rule is shared among demigods, each governing a portion of creation. If such beings possessed even a share within a defined domain, they would answer appeals concerning it. Finally, none is God’s helper, wholly or partly: God needs no aid to sustain and govern the universe, and a genuine assisting ruler would answer requests within its office. Thus their non-response negates all three alleged bases of their divinity: independent control, partnership with God, and assistance to Him.
verses.23:
Al-Mizan states that the intercession claimed by the idolaters is not the Qur’anically established intercession of the hereafter, since they did not believe in the hereafter. It is their claim that the beings they worshipped would plead with God in worldly affairs, securing their needs and remedying their problems. Since these beings are God’s creatures and wholly subject to Him, they cannot intercede independently; the decisive question is whether God has authorized their intercession.

Regarding “except for whom He allows,” the commentary distinguishes two readings of li-man. On one, li- denotes ownership, so that intercession benefits those seeking it from angels whom God has allowed to intercede. On the other, li- denotes causality, so it concerns those whom God permits to receive intercession. Al-Mizan accepts the latter, as Tafsīr al-Kashshāf does. The angels are intermediaries who carry out the divine command, and their intercession is limited both to matters God permits and to particular persons for whom He grants permission. Thus the verse has the sense of they only intercede for whom Allah wills (21:28), rather than none can intercede, except by His will (10:3): their intercessory capacity is not denied in itself, but is exercised only under specific divine authorization.

“Until [the time] when fear is removed from their hearts” refers, in context, to these angelic intercessors. Fuzzʿia means the removal of fazaʿ, a terror and constriction expressing their inward humility before their Lord. They await the divine command in this state, heedless of themselves and of everything besides Him; when the command reaches them, their fear is lifted and they enact it immediately, without procrastination. Their existence is thus wholly absorbed in receiving and executing God’s decree.

Their asking one another, “What did your Lord say?” shows that the angels have distinct ranks and groups. The command reaches some before others, and the higher deliver it to the lower, who obey them without delay; nevertheless, all are truly obeying God alone. Their answer, “The truth,” indicates that the divine decree is fixed and cannot be annulled or altered. “He is the High, the Great” concludes by affirming that even the honoured angels can only receive, convey, and carry out His true command.

The verse consequently refutes the notion that angels, though intermediaries and intercessors, are independent overlords able to give or withhold according to their own judgment. They intervene in creation only by special permission and do nothing apart from obedience.

Al-Mizan rejects other exegetical accounts as unsuitable interpretations of the verse, though some may have merit independently: that the fearful ones are idolaters on the Day of Judgment who then confess the truth; that angels fear the approach of recording angels and mistakenly suppose the Hour has come; that the terror occurred when Gabriel first brought revelation to Muḥammad after the interval since Jesus; or that angels were overwhelmed when revelation was sent to other angels and later learned it concerned beings other than themselves. The commentary holds that these readings fail when measured against the verse’s context and the preceding account of the angels’ relation to the divine command.
verses.24:
Al-Mizan presents this as an argument against worshipping demigods for sustenance. The idolaters hoped that worship would placate these beings and increase their provision, but provision from heaven and earth is itself created, and Allah alone is its Creator. Though the idolaters inwardly recognized this, they refused to acknowledge it openly; hence the Prophet is commanded to answer: Allah.

The statement that either side is on guidance or in manifest error is a fair summons to judge the opposing claims. Truth and falsehood, guidance and misguidance, admit no third alternative, so both parties cannot be right. The differing expressions reinforce this: one on guidance is like someone standing atop a lighthouse, able to see the way to happiness, whereas one in error is immersed in darkness, unable to know where to step or go.
verses.25: Al-Mizan explains that responsibility for evil deeds belongs exclusively to their doers: neither party will be questioned about the other’s acts. This prepares for the final gathering and judgment, where those who differ over right and wrong must be distinguished so that good and evil receive their due recompense from the exalted Lord. The verse courteously says “what you do” (taʿmalūn), rather than accusing the opponents of guilt.
verses.26:
Al-Mizan explains that resurrection gathers the doers of good and evil so that they may be distinguished and given the recompense due to their deeds. This gathering and true judgment belong to the Lord of both sides, the omniscient Arbiter who distinguishes all things in creation and governance.

The verse therefore establishes both the resurrection as a separation of the righteous from evildoers and the confinement of lordship to one Lord. The authority to distinguish people and recompense them cannot be distributed among a plurality of demigods, so the verse negates the lordship of those taken as lords besides God. Al-Fattāḥ, the Judge, denotes one who distinguishes things in their essences, attributes, and acts in order to set each in its proper order.
verses.27:
Al-Mizan explains that the Prophet is told to demand that the idolaters show the beings they have joined to God as partners, so that their alleged qualifications for divinity—independent life, knowledge, power, hearing, and sight—may be examined. Their visible idols are dead matter lacking these qualities. If they instead mean angels or other beings represented by the idols, such beings may possess God-given perfections but exercise none independently and cannot have divine functions delegated to them.

God’s infinite might prevents any creature from sharing His absolute perfection, lordship, or divinity. Nor can creatures be partners even without innate independence, for that would conflict with divine wisdom. Thus “Nay! He is Allah, the Mighty, the Wise” contains a decisive denial of both independent and non-independent partners.
verses.28:
Al-Mizan, following al-Rāghib, takes kāfiatan to mean a powerful restraint or shield: the Prophet was sent to keep people from wrongdoing, bringing glad tidings and warnings. The term derives from kaff, the hand and then the act of pushing away; its intensified ending conveys repeated and forceful restraint. The descriptions bashīr and nadhīr further clarify this meaning.

The commentary rejects construing kāffah as “all” and treating it as a descriptor of al-nās. That interpretation is grammatically convoluted, since it requires both that kāffah mean “all” and that a ḥāl precede what it describes while that noun is genitive (majrūr).

Though it speaks of prophethood, the verse is another proof of tawḥīd. A true Lord must guide people toward their happiness and ultimate end by sending a messenger. The universality of Muḥammad’s mission, as God’s messenger rather than anyone else’s, shows that lordship belongs exclusively to God: were there other lords, they would send their own messengers and dispute his universal mission. This is the point of the saying attributed to ʿAlī: “If your Lord had a partner, it would have sent its own messenger.” Most people do not perceive this implication—that the One who sends the Prophet to restrain people from sin through glad tidings and warnings is the sole Lord. And God knows best.
verses.29: Al-Mizan explains that the question asks when the resurrection and judgment, promised in “Say: Our Lord will gather us together; then He will decide between us in truth, and He is the Arbiter, the Knower (34:26),” will occur. Its connection with the surrounding argument also supports the commentary’s reading of (34:28) as a proof of tawḥīd rather than a merely separate discussion of prophethood; otherwise, verses 34:29–30 would interrupt the later passage on prophethood.
verses.30: Al-Mizan explains that the Prophet is to answer that the Resurrection has a fixed, pre-ordained, and unchangeable appointment, whose time God has decisively set but concealed from all others. The verse cannot concern an individual’s death, because the idolaters were asking about the Promised Day when people are gathered and judged, not about the moment of their deaths.
verses.31:
Al-Mizan identifies “those who disbelieve” as the idolaters, not the Jews, and “what came before it” as earlier divine scriptures such as the Torah and Gospel, since their denial of prophethood entailed denial of its scriptures. The interpretation that this phrase means the hereafter lacks evidence, whereas the Qur’an commonly uses it for the Torah and Gospel.

The verses portray the irreversible consequences of kufr caused by its leaders’ misguidance of their followers: at the Resurrection, those who rejected God’s Book and Messenger stand for reckoning and recompense, quarrelling and disowning one another. The Prophet is privately addressed by “Could you but see,” because the disbelievers were too obstinate to understand.

The downtrodden are followers, and the arrogant are their leaders, a distinct group indicated by al- in al-ẓālimūn. The followers charge that the leaders forced them into disbelief and kept them from faith. The leaders deny coercion: the Prophet’s guidance reached the followers, who chose disbelief and persisted in wrongdoing; thus they themselves bear responsibility.

verses.33:
Al-Mizan explains that the downtrodden reject the proud leaders’ claim of innocence: through continual plotting, the leaders weakened and dominated them until they obeyed commands to deny God and set up andādan, beings regarded as like God or similar demigods.

When punishment makes escape impossible, both parties conceal their regret. Although all secrets will then be exposed, their entrenched habit of lying and dissimulation remains: as they hid regret in worldly life to avoid enemies’ taunts, they still try to conceal it in the Hereafter, revealing themselves as habitual liars. Their deeds themselves become aghlāl, shackles around their necks that imprison them in punishment; this is their requital for what they did.
verses.34: Al-Mizan explains that al-mutrafūn are those luxuriously equipped, or rich. Their recurring denial of the warners’ message implies that wealth can foster arrogance before the truth.
verses.35:
Al-Mizan explains that the affluent deniers measure success solely by wealth and children, become attached to these fickle possessions, and forget what follows the material world. Since they regard deprivation of them as punishment, their continued possession makes them dismiss punishment in the Hereafter.

Blinded by wealth and offspring, they also infer that God has permanently granted them special honour. Thus their boast means that, even if there is a hell, God will not punish those to whom He has given such abundance. This resembles the claim: “This is mine, and I do not think the hour will come. If I am sent back to my Lord, I shall have good from Him. (41:50)”
verses.36:
Al-Mizan presents this as the first answer to the claim that wealth and children prove immunity from punishment. God alone expands or constricts sustenance, including wealth and children, for whichever servant He wills, according to wisdom and the greater good rather than human desire. Receiving abundance or scarcity therefore proves neither faith nor unbelief, prudence nor foolishness, and wealth is neither a guarantee of eternal happiness nor a token of honour.

God is called “My Lord” because the deniers did not recognize Him as their lord, while sustaining belongs to lordship. Most people do not know this: in want they ascribe their condition to accidental material causes, and in abundance to their own prudent management, rather than to the true giver.
verses.37:
Al-Mizan gives the second answer to the claim that wealth and children prevent punishment: nearness to God, not possessions or offspring, spares one from punishment. By saying that wealth and children do not bring people near God, the verse rhetorically states that what they relied on cannot save them from Hell.

Wealth and children benefit a believer who directs them to righteous ends: one spends wealth in God’s way and raises faithful, righteous children. Such a person receives a double reward and is secure in lofty dwellings. Perhaps the reward is called double because such people both are guided and guide others, or because good deeds are multiplied up to tenfold or more. Conversely, those who strive against God’s signs, seeking to weaken or outstrip Him, are summoned to punishment despite their possessions and children.

The address now applies generally: wealth and children benefit all who possess faith and use them righteously; otherwise, they bring only misery.

verses.39:
Al-Mizan, citing Majmaʿ al-Bayān, explains yukhlifuhu as God’s replacing what someone has spent or lost. The spending meant here is spending on a good cause, so it is not lost: whether much or little, and whatever form of wealth, God replaces it in this world or the next.

Sustenance lies wholly in God’s hands; His wealth neither decreases when He gives nor increases when He withholds. He is the best and true sustainer, giving openly rather than like people who expect an equivalent return; others are only intermediaries through whom His sustenance is delivered.
verses.40:
Al-Mizan holds that those gathered include worshippers and those worshipped. God’s question to the angels, “Were you what they worshipped?”, does not ask whether people in fact worshipped angels, for some did, though the angels abhorred it. It asks whether the angels consented to that worship, like the question put to Jesus in (5:116).

The question rebukes the idolaters and removes their hope that angels or other beings worshipped as intercessors will aid them.
verses.41:
Al-Mizan explains that the angels first glorify God, absolving Him of every blemish and thereby affirming, among other things, that none but Him merits worship. Rather than directly uttering the abhorrent denial that they allowed worship of themselves, they say that God alone is their waliyyunā. Since worship requires mutual guardianship, muwālāh, between worshipper and worshipped, God’s exclusive wilāyah means that no such relation existed between angels and humans and that the angels never assented to being worshipped.

The idolaters worshipped angels, jinn, and saints, regarding angels and jinn as most worthy of worship, although saints, having attained perfection, are superior to both. The jinn named here appear to be jinn whom idolaters considered the root of worldly evil and worshipped to avert evil, just as they worshipped angels greedily for their gifts and by way of barter. The wording indicates that these jinn accepted their worship.

Al-Mizan rejects the view that “jinn” means Iblīs and his descendants and that worship merely means obeying their incitement to evil: the verse says the idolaters had faith in the jinn, not merely obedience. It likewise does not say that jinn appeared as angels or entered idols. “Most,” rather than all, apparently reflects that most worshipped jinn to ward off evil; interpreting “most” as all rests on the mistaken equation of worship with obedience.
verses.42: Al-Mizan explains that, after the angels disclaim any desire to be worshipped, no one on that Day will have power to harm or help another. As elsewhere in the Qur’an, those who were made partners with God and their worshippers disavow one another; the tyrants are then told to taste the Fire they denied.
verses.43:
Al-Mizan explains that some idolaters responded to the clear verses—verses which rebuked their attachment to ancestral custom—by telling one another that the Prophet merely wished to turn them from what their fathers worshipped. The description of the signs as clear itself rebukes them: instead of calling people to evident truth, they fervently sought to bind them to their forefathers’ path.

Their “This is but a lie that is forged” refers dismissively to the Qur’anic āyāt, treating them as fabrications about God rather than clear signs sent down by Him; this shows that they understood nothing of them and regarded them as ordinary speech. Although truth reached them and became manifest, their kufr impelled them to call it clear sorcery and falsehood.
verses.44: Al-Mizan explains that this describes the Quraysh disbelievers’ baseless preference for personal desire over clear truth. They called truth sorcery although God had given them neither books by which they could distinguish truth from falsehood nor earlier warners or messengers whose scriptures or teaching could furnish such a claim.
verses.45:
Al-Mizan explains that the present Quraysh disbelievers possess not even a tenth of the power and might granted to earlier peoples, though both rejected God’s signs. When those earlier peoples denied God’s messengers, they were seized by His chastisement; how much weaker, then, are the Quraysh.

Miʿshār means a tenth, and nakīr here means divine disapproval manifested as chastisement. The shift from “We gave them” to “My messengers” magnifies the earlier peoples’ offence and inspires terror at being seized for it.
verses.46:
Al-Mizan takes “I exhort you” to mean “I advise you,” and “rise up for Allah” to mean stirring oneself for God and His noble face. Rising in pairs and alone means considering the matter two by two or individually, not as an unthinking mob, for the rabble suppresses truth and produces falsehood.

“There is no madness in your companion” is primarily a new negative statement, though mā may alternatively be read as interrogative or relative. “Your companion” is the Prophet, a reminder that they had known him for forty years before his mission and had never seen delusion, weak-mindedness, or any condition suggesting madness. They are therefore urged to think separately and honestly about his message: he has always been sound, honest, and trustworthy, and sincerely warns them of severe Resurrection punishment rather than deceiving them.
verses.47:
Al-Mizan explains that the Prophet seeks no wage for his mission: a payment that he took only to return to the people would not truly be a wage. The statement reassures them that prophethood is not a means to acquire wealth or power.

His reward is instead with God, answering the objection that a rational person does nothing without an end. God, who witnesses all things and the Prophet’s work, will provide that recompense rather than the people.
verses.48: Al-Mizan explains yaqdhifu as “casts” or “throws,” and ʿallām al-ghuyūb as either a second predicate or the predicate of a new, elided-subject sentence referring to God. In context, God’s casting forth of truth is the revelation of the Qur’an, which distinguishes truth from falsehood. Issued by the Knower of the unseen, it is truth hurled from the divine realm that smashes falsehood into oblivion.
verses.49: Al-Mizan identifies the truth that has come as the Qur’an, whose decisive arguments cut falsehood off at its root. “Falsehood neither creates nor restores” means that after truth comes it produces nothing new, and once it perishes it does not return; thus the Qur’an has eliminated it.
verses.50:
Al-Mizan explains that the truth in question is the Qur’an, the absolute truth which never fails to identify reality from every aspect; if it erred from any aspect, it would be falsehood in that respect. Divine revelation therefore guides and cannot misguide.

Accordingly, any error by the Prophet would arise from his own human soul and harm himself, whereas his guidance comes from what his Lord revealed and can only produce guidance. God is hearing and near: He hears prayers without distance, knows the unseen so that nothing escapes Him, and nothing can obstruct His will to guide people through revelation and safeguard its delivery.
verses.51:
Al-Mizan explains that these verses describe the Quraysh idolaters’ state at death. Terrified, they can neither flee God nor defend themselves or devise an escape. Their passive “seizure” means they are taken before God.

To be seized from a near place is a metaphor for God’s nearness to the human being: nothing separates them from the one taking them. God is nearer than people can perceive, closer than they are to their own souls, and His angels act under His direct command without veil or intermediary. Human beings require this metaphor because space, time, forgetfulness, and material distraction prevent them from comprehending that nearness; the reality is weightier still.
verses.52: Al-Mizan identifies “it” as the Qur’an and tanāwush as attaining. The “far place” is the Hereafter, the realm of recompense, far from the earthly realm in which people could strive and earn. There the seen and unseen have reversed: the world has vanished and the otherworld has appeared, so their professed faith cannot be attained in time.
verses.53:
Al-Mizan explains this as qualifying the question of how they can attain faith: while living, they disbelieved in the Qur’an and speculated without knowledge about the unseen Hereafter, denying resurrection, heaven, and hell. Some exegetes also take their conjecture to include accusing the Prophet of sorcery, lying, fabrication, and poetry.

Both the world and Hereafter are called far places because each is distant from the other. Once seized, the idolaters believe in the Qur’anic truth, but their new faith cannot save them in the now-present Hereafter, since in their now-distant earthly life they rejected life after death.
verses.54:
Al-Mizan states that, on the most apparent reading, what the idolaters desire is the worldly material pleasure from which death cuts them off. Their “likes” are earlier people like them or adherents of the same religious traditions. They are separated from these pleasures as earlier idolaters were, because those predecessors were in disquieting doubt about the truth or Hereafter and merely conjectured about the unseen.

This is the apparent interpretation. Numerous Shiʿi and Sunni narrations also report that these verses foretell the Sufyānī’s rising and the swallowing of his army by the earth at al-Baydāʾ, a sign of the Mahdī’s appearance; this is only one among the verse’s range of meanings.
